medical.label: Medical / Institutional
medical.ownership: Mixed. Hospitals are mostly nonprofit or government-owned (AHA 2026: 58% of community hospitals nonprofit, 24% investor-owned, 18% state/local government). Medical office buildings: over half of sq ft is owned by users (health systems, physician groups); about 37% is investor-owned (REITs about 35% of that, private investors about 65%).
medical.cap_rate_note: Default false because most hospitals and many clinics are owner-occupied or nonprofit and aren't valued on NOI/cap rate. Set true only for an investor-owned MOB (REIT or private landlord); then use cap_rates_by_market[market].medical_office (national about 6.8%-6.9%).

leak_consequence_multiplier.note: Multiplier scales reactive repair and storm-damage consequence costs relative to a warehouse (1.0). No insurer publishes water/roof-leak claim severity by occupancy relative to warehouses; value is a conservative PAX proposal, capped at 1.5 per model policy. Highest consequence type: any water intrusion over clinical space triggers an Infection Control Risk Assessment (ICRA) and often Class IV containment with negative pressure/HEPA exhaust (CDC, ASHE); sterile supplies, imaging and lab equipment can be lost; ORs, procedure rooms or patient rooms may close (lost revenue); Joint Commission EC.02.06.01 findings follow unsafe conditions. Insurers (Chubb, AXA XL) flag healthcare as a rising, high-severity water-loss class. One case: $200K property damage + $350K lost income from a roof-drain leak at a medical practice (PSQH excerpt). Kept at 1.4 (not 1.5) because the model also covers medical office buildings, where consequences are closer to office; use the high end (1.5) for acute-care hospitals.

medical.value_story: Lead with continuity of care and compliance, not property value: avoiding closed ORs, patient rooms and imaging suites; avoiding ICRA containment events and loss of sterile supplies/equipment; keeping Joint Commission Environment of Care (EC.02.06.01) survey findings clean; predictable capital budgets for health-system facilities teams. For investor MOBs, add tenant retention (long leases with health systems) and property value protected.

Built-up roofing (BUR)
Hybrid mod-bit base with TPO/PVC cap

k12.ownership: Public schools are owned by about 18,000 school districts (NCES CCD, about 100,000 public schools); private and parochial schools are owned by nonprofits or churches. Funded by bonds, capital levies and operating budgets, not by NOI.
k12.cap_rate_note: No NOI or market sale, so cap-rate valuation does not apply. Hide 'property value protected' and replace it with budget-certainty, avoided emergency spend and instructional days protected.

leak_consequence_multiplier.note: Multiplier scales reactive repair and storm-damage consequence costs relative to a warehouse (1.0). No insurer publishes water/roof-leak claim severity by occupancy relative to warehouses; value is a conservative PAX proposal, capped at 1.5 per model policy. Evidence of higher consequence: GAO found about 19% of districts canceled school in 2024-25 due to facility issues (2 million students, about 3.5 million lost learning days), and schools visited had ceiling, floor and electrical damage from roof leaks; EPA requires drying wet materials within 24-48 h or replacing them, and school mold events run from hundreds of thousands to millions (e.g., about $2.3M Nobleboro, ME, 2026). Classrooms have dense finishes, books and electronics; closures carry makeup-day and transport costs; public scrutiny raises remediation standards. Set below medical because schools can often relocate classes and many leaks occur outside occupied hours.

k12.value_story: Emphasize budget certainty and capital planning: a flat, predictable PaxSeal line item vs unbudgeted emergency repairs; extending roof life to defer bond-funded replacement; protecting instructional days (GAO: about 19% of districts canceled school in 2024-25 for facility problems, 2 million students affected); preventing mold/IAQ events (EPA: dry within 24-48 h); documented condition data for facility-condition assessments and bond planning. Context: national school facility funding gap about $85B/yr (2021 State of Our Schools); 41% of districts need HVAC updates in at least half their schools (GAO-20-494), so roofs compete for scarce capital.
typical_roof_systems: SBS modified bitumen (widely preferred by districts for redundancy)
Built-up roofing (BUR) on older buildings
TPO / PVC / EPDM single-ply
Hybrid mod-bit + single-ply

multifamily.label: Multi-Family
multifamily.ownership: Predominantly investor-owned (private owners, syndicators, REITs, institutional funds); some public housing authorities and nonprofits (LIHTC).
multifamily.cap_rate_note: Use cap_rates_by_market[market].multifamily (about 5.35%-6.0% across the five markets, 2026). Multifamily has the lowest cap rates of any type, so each $1 of NOI gain protects the most value (about $17-$19 per $1). For LIHTC/public housing, turn off cap-rate valuation.

leak_consequence_multiplier.note: Multiplier scales reactive repair and storm-damage consequence costs relative to a warehouse (1.0). No insurer publishes water/roof-leak claim severity by occupancy relative to warehouses; value is a conservative PAX proposal, capped at 1.5 per model policy. Top-floor units sit directly under the roof: a leak hits occupied living space (drywall, flooring, personal property), may force tenant relocation/rent abatement and unit downtime, and carries mold/habitability liability that is described as the fastest-growing multifamily risk (habitability premiums $375-$1,400/unit, up 300%+ in some markets per Bisnow excerpt). Offsetting factor: many garden-style roofs are steep-slope shingles with lower leak frequency, but frequency is handled elsewhere in the model; this multiplier covers consequence cost only.

multifamily.value_story: NOI and value: avoided repair spend flows to NOI and is capitalized at a low cap rate. Also stress resident retention (top-floor leaks trigger move-outs and bad reviews), avoided unit downtime/rent abatement, mold and habitability liability (fast-rising insurance line), and lender/insurer roof-age scrutiny (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac property condition reports).
typical_roof_systems: Architectural asphalt shingles on steep-slope garden-style and townhome buildings (most common low-rise type)
TPO single-ply on low-slope mid-rise/podium buildings
Modified bitumen / BUR on older low-slope buildings
Low-slope membrane sections over breezeways and stairwells on garden-style buildings
Standing-seam metal accents
multifamily.notes: Low-rise steep-slope shingle roofs may fall outside a low-slope commercial PaxSeal scope; mid-rise/podium roofs are low-slope. Roof-system excerpts: https://www.jm.com/en/commercial-roofing/building-owners/low-slope-roofing-for-multifamily-buildings/ ; https://windwardroofing.com/blog/multifamily-roofing-guide .

mixed.label: Mixed Use
mixed.ownership: Investor-owned (developers, private owners, funds), typically ground-floor retail with apartments or office above.
mixed.cap_rate_note: No broker publishes a mixed-use cap rate for these markets. Use an income-weighted blend: cap = w_retail x retail cap + (1 - w_retail) x upper-use cap (multifamily for residential-over-retail, office for office-over-retail). Default w_retail = 0.30 (PAX assumption for one retail floor under two to three upper floors; let the rep override). This matches how lenders and appraisers underwrite mixed use: split the rent roll by use, then recombine.

leak_consequence_multiplier.note: Multiplier scales reactive repair and storm-damage consequence costs relative to a warehouse (1.0). No insurer publishes water/roof-leak claim severity by occupancy relative to warehouses; value is a conservative PAX proposal, capped at 1.5 per model policy. No direct evidence; derived as a blend of the components. The roof sits over the upper use (apartments or office, 1.2-1.25), not the ground-floor retail, so the default follows the upper use: 1.2 (office-over-retail) to 1.25 (apartments-over-retail). Use 1.25 when the upper floors are residential.

mixed.value_story: Same NOI/value story as the dominant upper use, plus: the roof protects the residential/office floors directly, and leaks can cascade to ground-floor retail tenants (business interruption, co-tenancy risk). One maintenance program protects several income streams.
typical_roof_systems: TPO / PVC single-ply on low-slope podium or wrap buildings
Modified bitumen
Amenity decks / pavers over membrane on podium roofs
Occasional steep-slope shingle or metal accents
mixed.notes: Blend approach per mixed-use underwriting guides (search excerpts): https://www.rentalcalcs.com/blog/analyzing-mixed-use-property-residential-commercial ; https://peersense.com/cmbs-loans/mixed-use .

leak_consequence_multiplier.note: Baseline by definition. Warehouses have high ceilings, sparse finishes and few occupants per sq ft, so leak consequences are mostly the roof repair itself plus stored-goods exposure.
